desc: magus agent install writes the skills and the AGENTS.md block, and magus describe harness prints the hook entries a person merges into the host's config. From then on the host runs the guard's PreToolUse hook before every shell command, file edit and magus MCP call, and only an allowed call runs. Skills, guard verdicts and MCP replies all name commands through internal/hint, so a renamed command cannot leave one of them pointing at nothing.
title: What an agent host gets, and the gate every call crosses

desc: In a checkout with no ./magus, the guard's raw-tool rule advises exactly one command through, alone on its line: GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2 go run -trimpath ./cmd/magus run go-build --no-cache ., which runs the real go-build target. It regenerates the spell bytecode first and links a stamp of the sources the binary was built from. Every other raw go command, a bare go build included, is refused and served that command; once ./magus exists the rule names ./magus run go-build . instead. The magus on PATH re-execs that ./magus; the stale policy compares its stamp with the checkout, and when a binary can no longer load the tree the same bootstrap is allowed over it, which is the one way back.
title: One go run, then magus builds magus

desc: Session.Exec compiles source in six steps, all in the gopherbuzz root package except the first and the last. The lexer, token.Tokenize, turns the source into tokens; a session given a parse cache keeps them by source text, so a module many sessions import is lexed once. The parser builds an ast.Program. Before the checker sees it, import resolution runs every imported file through this same pipeline and the VM, so their exports are bound when the checker looks names up. The checker reports types.Type mismatches as BZZ diagnostics, and the compiler emits a vm.Chunk, one per function. In the vm package, FoldConsts folds constants and FusePeephole fuses the common local, constant and branch sequences into superinstructions. A session with a bytecode store saves the chunk with every file it was compiled against and, on a later run where all of them still hold the same bytes, hands the saved chunk to the VM without parsing anything.
title: From Buzz source to a chunk

desc: Every Buzz program magus touches goes through the same gopherbuzz pipeline: lex, parse, check, compile, run. Hosts differ only in the modules they register first. The host bindings attach to the magusfile engine at init and provide every magus host module, each through the trampoline generated from its descriptor. The browser playground runs the dry evaluator, which installs only the trampolines marked WASM, pure compute with no filesystem, process or network access, and records host calls instead of running them. Both also install the Buzz stdlib.
title: One pipeline, and the modules each host registers

desc: Session.runChunk makes a VM and calls VM.Run with the chunk and the session's environment. Run reserves the top-level register window and asks jitRun first. With the JIT on, the baseline JIT judges the chunk once and caches the verdict: depths() admits only the numeric subset, locals, constants, arithmetic, comparisons and jumps, and validates every operand, and compileJIT emits amd64 or arm64 code through golang-asm into executable pages. Only the chunk Run was handed can go native; a function it calls runs on the interpreter. There is one native tier and no hotness counter. A value the native code cannot handle deopts to the interpreter at the instruction it stopped on, with the stack depth checked; a chunk the JIT declines, or one with no slot locals, runs on the interpreter from the start. The interpreter's values are NaN-boxed 64-bit words, and heap objects are handles into one table the session releases when it closes.
title: Interpreter first, native code when the chunk allows it

desc: A pull request run reads the signed remote tier and reads and writes a local tier scoped to its own ref. Only a run on the default branch holds the signing key, so only the default branch writes the remote tier. Every read checks the signature and rebuilds the target on an unsigned entry.
title: A pull request reads the shared cache and never writes it

desc: A ci target names its steps in a single needs call, so they are independent and run in parallel. Order comes from edges the steps themselves declare, such as test depending on build. magus enforces none of this list.
title: ci declares steps, not an order

desc: A failing project reaches the annotator contract, which speaks generic verbs to a provider spell; the spell translates them into the CI system's own syntax. Quote prefixes are declared once and applied per line in Go.
title: Vendor syntax lives in the spell, never in the binary

desc: A generated file is committed only when it is a pure function of committed sources, is not already produced by the build, is read by something that never runs the build, and is neither large nor churning.
title: Whether a generated file belongs in the repo

desc: A figure in docs/site/diagrams builds its boxes from the knowledge graph's own records, magus\dir, magus\dirs and magus\layer, and draws the imports and declared calls between them. magus/figure lays it out and paints it; diagrams-generate writes the committed light, dark and page copies with a receipt beside each, and the site render inlines the page copy. The server embeds the same module to draw live figures at /api/v1/diagrams, which the console fetches.
title: One library draws every figure, here and in the console

desc: Almost every CI job builds magus from the commit under test and runs it against that commit's magusfile, so a change can rely on a feature that has not shipped. One audit job instead runs the pinned previous release against the same magusfile; it is advisory, and a failure reports a breaking change rather than blocking the branch.
title: magus builds magus, then runs the last release at it too

desc: The host's PreToolUse hook, wired by magus agent harness install, pipes the event to magus shell. The built-in rules judge it first, reading the job store for the lease the call acts as; the workspace's magus\guard.command rule sees only what they let through and can only add to the verdict. A deny carries its reason and a next: breadcrumb naming the command to run instead, and the hook renders it into the host's reply.
title: One command judges every call, and says what to run instead

desc: Without the cd charm an image-build loads locally and pushes nothing. With it, the channel decides: the default commit channel adds one immutable tag to one registry, and only stable moves the floating latest tag.
title: What a bare run pushes, and what each channel adds

desc: A target's ctx.readsFiles and ctx.writesFiles globs resolve from its own project's directory. The source walk matches every file a glob names, so the root's **/*.go keys every nested Go file too. An output glob claims a file inside a nested project only when the glob is rooted there; the snapshot, the replay and the drift gate all ask the same rule, and a write that lands there anyway fails the run as MGS3001. A nested project reads the root's tree through a project handle, workspace\file, which also makes the root its upstream. The matched files and the probed tool versions are the key; an input nobody declared never reaches it.
title: An output stops at a nested project; an input does not

desc: magus graph build assembles a shard per source: the registry and one per project from the magusfiles, the file adapters for Buzz, docs, directories, citations and CODEOWNERS, a lazy symbol shard per project from a SCIP index, git history and notes. The store fingerprints each shard and rewrites only the ones whose content changed, then merges them into one graph. The CLI and the MCP tools read that graph through the same query, explain, refs and path.
title: Every source writes a shard; every reader asks one graph

desc: An orchestrator checkpoints the working state, partitions the work by write set using graph evidence, and forks one job per unit: goal, checkpoint, write paths. Holders release paths as soon as they are done with them, so the plan shrinks while it runs, and the Jobs view renders the rows, their overlaps and their staleness for whoever is watching. The orchestrator verifies each job by diffing since that job's checkpoint against what it claimed, then integrates and runs magus affected ci. magus records and answers; it enforces none of it.
title: A declared plan, released early, verified by diff

desc: For a conflicted file the queue asks the classifier which class the edit is and settles only a low-risk one, kicking code back, then gates the projects the magus SDK says the change reaches, or every project when that set is no proof.
title: What a candidate's risk makes the queue run

desc: magus accepts a workspace URL, a workspace-relative path, a dot-relative path or the bare root alias, and parses them all to one project reference. Human output prints the short path; machine output prints the workspace URL.
title: Four spellings in, one reference out

desc: Agents and the console reach /mcp, the /api/v1 read views, the review and plan routes and the typed Connect services through the DNS-rebind, bearer-token and CORS guard. POST /api/v1/diff/session carries the human half of a paired review and POST /api/v1/share opens the LAN listener; both are loopback only. The health endpoints answer probes directly, with no authentication.
title: The HTTP routes, and the one route without a guard

desc: File changes drive the watchers and the SCIP auto-indexer; a magus run queues a coalesced graph-build job. All three write into the workspace registry, which is the server's single warm copy of the knowledge graph.
title: What keeps the warm workspace current

desc: Sharing from the dashboard posts to a loopback-only endpoint, which mints a time-boxed read-only token and opens an ephemeral LAN listener. The listener serves four JSON read routes and the read Connect services, and nothing else: the graph, the diff routes, the derived plan, the job store, /mcp and job control stay loopback only.
title: The only listener a second machine can reach

desc: The magus CLI dispatches over a private unix domain socket into the concurrency pool, the workspace registry and the run registry; shared services go to the broker. Sharing a graph spawns a separate short-lived loopback server.
title: How a local command reaches the server

desc: magus refuses a ci run when no project in scope declares ci. Every other step, and the order between them, is the convention this workspace follows so each verb means the same thing in every project.
title: Only ci is required; the rest is an order

desc: A failing target that opted in is retried once while its history is too thin to judge, when the diff did not touch its project, or when its measured volatility is above the threshold. A retry that passes is recorded as volatile and the run continues; anything else is a suspected regression.
title: When a failure is retried, and when it is believed

desc: Discovery walks the tree from the root marker and registers one project per magusfile: the root's is project ., each nested one declares its own. Every magusfile is evaluated: its exported functions are its targets and magus\project layers policy on. A static read of each target body recovers ctx.readsFiles, ctx.writesFiles and cross-project ctx.needs as literals. The project model that results is what the cache keys, what describe answers from, and what a command resolves its project against from the current directory.
title: A target exists because a magusfile exported it
